title: Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp
description: A poor boy finds a magic lamp and wins a princess, outwitting an evil magician.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There once lived in China a poor tailor with his wife and son Aladdin, a careless, idle boy. When his father died, Aladdin idled in the streets. One day a stranger, a magician from Africa, claimed to be his uncle and hired him. He led Aladdin to a lonely place, lit a fire, and threw powder on it, and the earth opened, showing steps down to treasure. 'Go down,' said the magician, 'and bring me the old lamp you will find. Touch nothing else.' Aladdin descended, saw gardens of jewel fruits, and found the lamp. But when he tried to climb out, the magician demanded the lamp first, and Aladdin refused until he was out. In anger the magician sealed the earth, leaving Aladdin trapped. Weeping, Aladdin wrung his hands, and rubbed a ring the magician had lent him. A genie appeared: 'I am the slave of the ring. What is your wish?' Aladdin wished to be home, and was instantly transported. His mother cleaned the lamp, and rubbing it, summoned a mightier genie, slave of the lamp, who could grant any wish. With the genie's help, Aladdin grew rich, built a splendid palace, and won the Sultan's daughter, the Princess Badroulbadour, for his wife. The magician, learning of this, returned in disguise as a lamp-seller crying 'New lamps for old!' The princess, not knowing the lamp's value, traded it. The magician commanded the genie to carry the palace and princess to Africa. Aladdin, in despair, rubbed the ring, and its genie carried him to Africa. There Aladdin had the princess drug the magician's wine; while he slept, Aladdin seized the lamp, and commanded its genie to return the palace to China. The magician was executed, and Aladdin and his princess lived happily, and at the Sultan's death Aladdin succeeded to the throne.

title: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
description: Ali Baba learns 'Open, Sesame!' and his slave Morgiana defeats forty thieves.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Ali Baba was a poor woodcutter who lived with his wife in Persia. His rich brother Cassim married well, but Ali Baba remained poor. One day in the forest, Ali Baba saw forty horsemen. He hid in a tree and watched their captain stand before a rock and say: 'Open, Sesame!' The rock opened into a cave full of treasure. The thieves loaded their horses and left, the captain saying 'Shut, Sesame!' After they left, Ali Baba tried the words, entered, and took some gold coins. He told his wife, who borrowed a measure from Cassim's wife to measure the gold. Cassim's wife put wax in the measure to learn what was measured, and found gold stuck to it. Cassim forced Ali Baba to reveal the secret, went to the cave, but forgot the magic words in his greed and was trapped. The thieves found him and killed him. Ali Baba fetched his brother's body, and his clever slave Morgiana sewed it together so none would know. The thieves sought revenge. Their captain, disguised as an oil merchant, lodged with Ali Baba, hiding thirty-seven thieves in oil jars in the courtyard. Morgiana, fetching oil, heard a thief whisper from a jar, and answered all the jars, learning the plot. That night she boiled oil and poured it into each jar, killing the thieves. When the captain came to rouse them and found them dead, he fled. Later he returned disguised as a merchant, but Morgiana recognized him and stabbed him during a dance she performed. Ali Baba freed Morgiana and married her to his son. And so the forty thieves were defeated by a slave girl's wit.

title: The Seven Voyages of Sinbad the Sailor
description: Sinbad survives whales, rocs, giants and cannibals across seven voyages.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Sinbad the Sailor told his story to Sinbad the Porter. On his first voyage, his ship landed on what seemed an island but was a great whale; when fires were lit, it dived, and Sinbad was saved on a plank, reaching an island where he served a king and grew rich. On his second voyage, he was left on an island and found the egg of the roc, a giant bird; he tied himself to its leg and was carried to a valley of diamonds, where he gathered wealth and was rescued by merchants. On his third voyage, his crew was captured by a giant cannibal who ate them one by one; Sinbad blinded the giant with heated spits and escaped on rafts. On his fourth voyage, his ship wrecked among cannibals who fed travelers a maddening herb; Sinbad refused it, escaped, and found a civilized kingdom where he married. On his fifth voyage, his men broke a roc's egg and the parent rocs destroyed the ship with rocks; Sinbad reached the island of the Old Man of the Sea, who rode on his shoulders until Sinbad made him drunk and killed him, winning great riches. On his sixth voyage, his ship was wrecked near a subterranean river; Sinbad built a raft and floated through a mountain into a land of precious stones, and returned home rich. On his seventh and last voyage, after being enslaved and escaping winged men and other perils, Sinbad returned to Baghdad, rich beyond measure, and gave the porter a hundred sequins, bidding him cease his labors. And so Sinbad ended his voyages.

title: The Fisherman and the Genie
description: A fisherman tricks a vengeful genie back into its jar and is rewarded.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: There was once a poor old fisherman who cast his net four times a day and no more. One day he cast his net and drew up a dead donkey; the second time, a jar of mud; the third time, broken pots. In despair he cast a fourth time, and drew up a copper vessel sealed with lead, stamped with Solomon's seal. He opened it, and a great genie rose in smoke. The genie had been imprisoned by Solomon for rebellion, and vowed to kill whoever freed him after the first centuries passed. 'Choose how you will die,' said the genie. The fisherman trembled, but thought of a trick. 'I cannot believe,' he said, 'that one so great as you could fit in so small a vessel.' 'See for yourself,' said the genie, and turned to smoke and re-entered the jar. The fisherman quickly sealed it. The genie begged for mercy, promising riches, and the fisherman, after making him swear by Solomon's name, freed him. The genie led him to a pond of colored fishes — white, red, blue, yellow — and bade him take them to the Sultan. The Sultan's cook fried one, and a wall opened, and a maiden asked the fish to keep its oath; the fish answered, and the maiden overturned the pan. The Sultan investigated and found the pond was once a city, its people enchanted into fishes by a wicked magician, and its young king half marble. The Sultan freed the city, married the king's sister, and made the fisherman his treasurer. And the fisherman lived in honor all his days.

title: The Merchant and the Genie
description: Three old men's tales ransom a merchant from a genie's vengeance.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A merchant, riding to collect debts, stopped to eat dates by a spring. He threw the stones aside, and one struck the son of a genie, killing him. The genie appeared with a great scimitar, vowing to kill the merchant. 'Give me a year,' begged the merchant, 'to settle my affairs and bid farewell.' The genie agreed. A year later the merchant returned to the spot to die. As he waited, three old men came up, each with an animal. The first old man, leading a hind, begged the genie to spare one third of the merchant's life if his story was wonderful. He told how his wife, jealous of his concubine, had turned the concubine into a hind and his son into a calf; how he had nearly sacrificed the calf, then learned the truth from a herdsman's daughter, restored them, and turned his wicked wife into the hind he led. The genie, pleased, granted a third. The second old man, with two black dogs, told how his brothers, envious of his wealth, threw him into the sea; a genie saved him but turned his brothers into dogs for three years, and his wife, who knew magic, was turned into a hind for trying to kill him. The genie granted another third. The third old man told of his wife's infidelity and his own adventures. The genie, delighted with all three stories, freed the merchant entirely. And the merchant returned home in joy.

title: The Ebony Horse
description: A prince flies an enchanted ebony horse to win a distant princess.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: On a festival day, three sages came before a king of Persia, each bearing a marvelous gift. One brought a golden peacock that struck the hours; another, a golden trumpet; the third, an ebony horse with a peg in its neck that could fly through the air. The king's son, Prince Kamar, mounted the horse to try it, turned the peg, and was carried aloft before he learned the secret of descending. He turned another peg and descended in a strange land. There he found a beautiful princess, and they fell in love. But her father, the king of that land, demanded impossible bride-prices. The prince returned on the horse to Persia, fetched treasures, and came back. The jealous sage who made the horse claimed it, and the king gave it to him, but the prince, by a trick, regained the horse and flew away with the princess to Persia, where they married. The sage pursued them, but the prince, turning the peg, caused the horse to trample the sage to death. And the prince and princess lived in happiness, and the ebony horse was kept as a wonder.

title: The Three Kalandars
description: Three one-eyed beggars and three ladies trade tales in Baghdad.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Haroun Al-Raschid, Caliph of Baghdad, walked the city by night in disguise with his vizier. They met three kalandars, each blind in the right eye, and a porter, and were invited to the house of three ladies. The ladies made them promise to ask no questions. During the evening, the ladies beat two dogs and then wept over them; a lady sang and tore her clothes; and the kalandars each told his tale. The first kalandar was a prince whose cousin, in love with him, tried to kill his wife; wars followed, and he was blinded by a vengeful vizier. The second was a prince turned to stone by a jealous magician, freed by a kind fairy, but blinded in one eye as the price. The third was a prince shipwrecked and enslaved, who escaped many perils but lost an eye to a roc. Then the ladies told their stories: the eldest had beaten the dogs, who were her sisters turned to dogs by a genie for cruelty; the second had torn her clothes in grief for a lost lover. The Caliph revealed himself, freed the sisters from the spell, married the eldest lady himself, married the others to the kalandars, and made the porter his steward. And all lived happily, and asked no more questions.

title: The Porter and the Three Ladies of Baghdad
description: The Caliph in disguise unravels the mystery of the three ladies.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A porter was hired by a beautiful lady to carry provisions to a great house in Baghdad, where two other ladies lived. They feasted him, and made him promise to ask no questions whatever he saw. In the evening, they brought in two black dogs, which one lady beat with a whip, weeping the while; then another lady sang a song so sorrowful that she tore her garments. Three kalandars knocked, each blind in the right eye, and were admitted on the same condition. Then the Caliph Haroun Al-Raschid knocked, disguised as a merchant, with his vizier and executioner. All promised silence. But when the ladies demanded the stories of all, the Caliph threatened punishment for curiosity. At last the ladies explained: the dogs were their sisters, enchanted; the singing lady mourned her lover. The Caliph, revealing himself, summoned the genie who had enchanted the sisters and forced him to restore them. He married the eldest, gave the others in marriage to his sons, made the porter his steward, and pardoned the kalandars. And the house of the three ladies became a place of joy.

title: The Little Hunchback
description: A dead hunchback is passed from door to door in a comedy of terrors.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A tailor and his wife invited a merry hunchback to supper. The hunchback laughed so hard at a joke that he choked on a fish bone and died. Fearing blame, the tailor carried the body to a doctor's house and left it on the stairs; the doctor, stumbling over it in the dark, thought he had killed his patient, and threw the body from his terrace into a neighbor's courtyard. The neighbor, a steward, thinking the hunchback was a thief, beat the corpse and carried it to the market, leaning it against a shop. A drunken Christian, thinking the hunchback was accosting him, struck him, and the body fell. The watch arrested the Christian for murder. At the gallows, each person in turn confessed to the 'murder' — the tailor, the doctor, the steward — each telling his tale. The Sultan, amazed, demanded the whole story, laughed till he swooned, and pardoned them all. He ordered the tales written in gold, and the hunchback was buried with honor. And the Sultan declared that the story of the hunchback was more wonderful than any he had heard.

title: Noureddin and the Fair Persian
description: Two lovers flee the Caliph and are reunited after many trials.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: The Caliph Haroun Al-Raschid had a beautiful slave, the Fair Persian, whom he gave to his son. But the vizier's son Noureddin saw her and fell in love, and she with him. They fled to Bussorah, where Noureddin's father was governor. But the Caliph, in anger, sent for them. On the way, they stopped at an inn, where Noureddin, drinking, fell asleep, and the Fair Persian was stolen by robbers. She was sold and resold, till at last she came into the hands of a king who would marry her. But she refused all food till Noureddin should be found. Noureddin, waking, searched the world for her. At last he came to the city where she was, and became a gardener's boy. The Fair Persian saw him from her window and recognized him. By a trick with a lamp, she summoned him to her. The king, learning the truth, was generous: he freed them, gave them gifts, and sent them back to Baghdad, where the Caliph pardoned them. And Noureddin and the Fair Persian lived together in happiness.

title: Prince Camaralzaman and the Princess Badoura
description: Two lovers meet only in sleep until fate reunites them across kingdoms.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: King Schahzaman had a son, Camaralzaman, so beautiful that the very sun was abashed. The king wished him to marry, but the prince refused, despising women. A genie and a genie's daughter disputed which was more beautiful, Camaralzaman or the Princess Badoura of China. They brought the sleepers together, and each woke and saw the other, and fell in love, exchanging rings before being carried back. Camaralzaman woke lovesick, and fell ill. His father built him a tower, where he pined. Meanwhile Badoura, likewise lovesick, was thought mad. At last a magician's trick brought them word of each other. Camaralzaman set out, and by many adventures reached China, where he became a gardener's assistant. Badoura, still pining, was visited by Camaralzaman's ring in a bird's crop, and knew he was near. They were reunited and married. On their voyage home, a storm separated them; Badoura, disguised as a man, became king of a distant island, and Camaralzaman, after many trials, came there and recognized her by a talisman. They returned to their kingdom and reigned in happiness, and their sons after them.

title: The Young King of the Black Isles
description: A betrayed king, half marble, is freed when a sultan outwits his wicked queen.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A king of the Black Isles, young and handsome, was betrayed by his wicked wife, who loved a black slave. When the king wounded the slave, the queen turned the king's lower half to marble, turned his city into a lake and his people into colored fishes, and tormented him daily with a hundred lashes. A sultan, hunting, discovered the lake of colored fishes and the young king. The sultan slew the queen's lover and tricked the queen: disguised, he made her break her own spells, restoring the king and his people. The queen herself was slain, and the young king, freed from marble and from torment, thanked the sultan and reigned in peace. And the lake remained no more, but the city stood again, and the fishes became men.

When the king wounded the slave, the queen turned the king's lower half to marble, turned his city into a lake and his people into colored fishes, and tormented him daily with a hundred lashes. A sultan, hunting, discovered the lake of colored fishes and the young king. The sultan slew the queen's lover and tricked the queen: disguised, he made her break her own spells, restoring the king and his people. The queen herself was slain, and the young king, freed from marble and from torment, thanked the sultan and reigned in peace. And the lake remained no more, but the city stood again, and the fishes became men.

title: Judar and His Brothers
description: A poor fisherman's magic saddlebag survives his brothers' treachery.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Judar was a poor fisherman with two envious brothers. One day he drew up in his net a Jew of great wealth, who promised him riches if he would help him find a treasure. They journeyed to a mountain, where, by magic words, a lake parted, revealing treasure guarded by enchanted men. Judar's brothers, jealous, tried to kill him, but the Jew saved him and gave him a magic saddlebag that produced food and a magic ring. Judar became rich and generous, but his brothers stole the talismans and had him imprisoned. The Jew freed him, restored the talismans, and punished the brothers. Judar married the Jew's daughter, lived in splendor, and forgave his brothers, who at last repented. And the magic saddlebag fed the poor of the city all Judar's days.

title: Ma'aruf the Cobbler
description: A poor cobbler's magic ring survives debt, a shrewish wife and thieves.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Ma'aruf was a poor cobbler of Cairo, whose shrewish wife made his life miserable. Fleeing from her, he traveled far and came to a city where, by a misunderstanding, he was taken for a rich merchant. Ashamed to confess, he kept up the pretense, borrowing to lend, till he was deep in debt. In despair he fled to a desert garden, where he found a magic ring whose genie gave him boundless wealth. He returned, paid his debts, and married the king's daughter. But his wife discovered the ring and stole it, fleeing with a lover. Ma'aruf pursued them, regained the ring by a trick, and punished the traitors. He returned to his princess, and they lived in splendor. And his first wife, hearing of his fortune, came to claim him, but the princess had her driven away, and Ma'aruf knew peace at last.

title: Abu Hassan, or the Sleeper Awakened
description: The Caliph makes a young man 'caliph for a day' as a splendid jest.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Abu Hassan, a rich young man of Baghdad, loved to entertain strangers. The Caliph Haroun Al-Raschid, disguised, was his guest, and amused by Abu Hassan's wish to be caliph for a day to punish the imams. The Caliph drugged his wine, carried him to the palace, and had him treated as caliph for a day. Abu Hassan, waking in splendor, believed himself caliph, held court, and punished the imams. At day's end he was drugged again and returned home. Waking poor, he believed it a dream, but told the tale so often that all thought him mad, and he was confined. The Caliph, repenting, freed him, told the truth, and made him his companion. Abu Hassan married a beautiful slave, and they contrived a trick: each pretended to die, to get funeral gifts from the Caliph and his wife. The trick was discovered, all laughed, and the Caliph heaped them with favors. And Abu Hassan never again wished to be caliph.

title: The Barber's Sixth Brother
description: A poor brother turns a rich man's mock feast into real fortune.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: The barber told the Caliph of his six brothers. The sixth, Schacabac, was a poor man who begged his living. One day a rich Barmecide invited him to dinner as a jest, and pretended to serve a feast, with empty dishes, praising each imaginary course. Schacabac, entering into the jest, pretended to eat and drink, and at last pretended to be drunk, and boxed the Barmecide's ears. The Barmecide laughed, confessed the jest, and served a real feast. Schacabac stayed, and was given money. But misfortune followed: he was robbed, beaten, and at last, leaping from a window to escape a fire, was impaled and lamed. He became a beggar again, and shaved for a living, like his brother the barber. And the Caliph laughed at the tale, and gave the barber gifts, and pardoned his chatter.

title: Sidi Nouman
description: A man discovers his wife is a ghoul and is turned into a dog.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Sidi Nouman married a beautiful wife, Amina, but noticed she ate only rice, grain by grain, with a bodkin. Following her one night, he saw her go to a graveyard and feast on dead bodies with a ghoul. Horrified, he refused to live with her. Amina, in revenge, turned him into a dog by sprinkling water on him. As a dog he was taken in by a baker, and one day saw a woman buying bread with false money; he barked, exposing her. The baker's daughter, skilled in magic, restored him to manhood, and turned Amina into a mare. Sidi Nouman, as advised, sold the mare with the condition she never be unsaddled, lest she resume her shape. And so the ghoul-wife remained a mare, and Sidi Nouman lived free.

title: The Blind Man, Baba Abdalla
description: A greedy beggar's magic ointment blinds him for his ingratitude.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Baba Abdalla was once rich, but giving all to a dervish, he became a beggar. The dervish, grateful, showed him a treasure in the mountains, bidding him take only what he could carry and ask for nothing more. But Baba Abdalla's greed grew; he begged for the dervish's magic ointment that revealed treasure. The dervish warned him to apply it only to one eye, but Baba Abdalla applied it to both and was struck blind. He returned to Baghdad, begging, and the Caliph heard his tale. 'I was punished,' said Baba Abdalla, 'for ingratitude and greed.' And he begs to this day, striking his own cheek with each alms, in penance.

title: The Two Sisters Who Were Jealous
description: A Talking Bird exposes jealous sisters who stole a queen's babies.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: A sultan, hearing three sisters wish — one for the baker, one for the cook, one for the sultan himself — married the youngest. She bore him a son, but her jealous sisters put the babe in a basket and set it afloat, replacing it with a puppy. Twice more this happened, with a kitten and a mole. The sultan, believing his wife a monster, imprisoned her. The three children were saved by a gardener, and grew up beautiful. The eldest sister, now married, visited them and, jealous still, told the daughter of three wonders: the Talking Bird, the Singing Tree, and the Golden Water. The sons fetched them at great peril, the youngest son nearly turned to stone. With the wonders, their home became paradise. The sultan visited, heard the Talking Bird tell the whole tale, freed his wife, and punished the jealous sisters. And the family was reunited in joy.

title: The Adventures of Haroun Al-Raschid
description: The Caliph in disguise rights wrongs in the night streets of Baghdad.
author: Traditional (Arabian Nights)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: The Caliph Haroun Al-Raschid often walked Baghdad by night in disguise with his vizier Giafar and his executioner Mesrour. One night they found a basket floating in the Tigris containing the body of a murdered woman, cut in pieces. The Caliph demanded the murderer in three days, on pain of the vizier's death. Giafar despaired, but on the third day a young man confessed: he had killed his wife in jealousy, though she was innocent. An old man then claimed the guilt, to save the youth — he was the wife's father, and had misled the husband with a lie about an apple. The Caliph, moved, pardoned both, and made the young man his gardener. Another night, the Caliph heard a lady lamenting, and found a tale of love and magic. And many such adventures befell Haroun Al-Raschid, who righted wrongs and showed mercy, and his name is blessed in Baghdad to this day.
